**First check rear sag against Honda’s 105 mm target with the standard shock spring.** Too little sag leaves the rear high and prone to kicking. Check chain slack and that the linkage moves freely before tuning around it.

Then use how it kicks to choose the adjustment:
- **First bump feels okay, then it gets lower and kicks harder:** open shock rebound **2 clicks from where it is now**. The shock needs to recover between bumps.
- **Straight-up kick immediately after one bump:** close shock rebound **2 clicks from where it is now** to slow its return.
- **Sharp sideways deflection:** compression is the more likely direction—not automatically rebound.

Honda’s standard shock rebound reference is **11–14 clicks out**, counting the first click as position 1; record your actual position before changing it.

Does it kick straight up or sideways, and is the first bump bad or does it build through the series?

For the retest, stay standing with knees bent, hips over the pegs and hands light. Ride the same braking section for three controlled passes, changing only one setting; undo the change if it kicks harder or loses grip.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Rear rider sag:** Measure first; if incorrect, set to 105 mm with the standard shock spring.
- **Shock rebound—choose only the matching branch:** If kicking builds through the series, open 2 clicks from the current position. If it kicks straight up immediately after one bump, close 2 clicks instead.
Check rear sag first; if the kick builds through successive braking bumps, try shock rebound 2 clicks farther out—not slower.

The fix changes with **on-throttle versus braking headshake**—softening the fork can help one and worsen the other. Testers consistently report this CRF450R generation is nervous at speed and sensitive to small setup changes.

Before another fast run, check steering-head bearing play or notchiness, front-wheel bearings, spokes and tire condition. If the bars swap violently or anything is loose, stop riding until corrected.

For stock suspension, Honda’s reference is **105 mm rider sag**, fork compression **10 clicks out** and fork rebound **13 clicks out**. Measure sag before chasing damping; too little sag can make the bike nose-down and nervous.

Common-practice tests, only after those checks:
- **On the gas, with the front skipping over bumps:** fork compression 1 click farther out from its current position, for better compliance.
- **Under braking, with the fork diving:** fork compression 1 click farther in from its current position, for more support.

Does it start while accelerating, holding steady throttle, or rolling off/braking? Leave rebound alone until that’s separated, and test only one change at a time.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork compression—only if skipping under acceleration:** From the current position to 1 click farther out, both legs equally; never exceed 16 clicks out.
- **Fork compression—alternative only if diving under braking:** From the current position to 1 click farther in, both legs equally.
Check the front end for play before another fast run. Whether the shake starts on the gas or under braking decides the damping change.

The shock is likely returning too slowly between hits—each whoop catches it before it has extended again.

**Shock rebound: go 1 click farther out from your current setting.** If it’s at Honda’s stock 11 clicks out, try 12 clicks out. That speeds up the return; don’t slow rebound further to cure this symptom.

First rule out an overly tight chain or sticky linkage, which can mimic packing. If sag hasn’t been set, Honda’s target with the standard shock spring is **105 mm**.

Retest the same manageable section for three passes at the same controlled pace. You want the rear to maintain its height without springing upward after each hit. Return that click if it starts bucking or feels loose.

Keep standing with your hips slightly back, knees gripping and throttle steady—not hanging off the rear fender. Use small, rounded whoops for the test; don’t add speed to mask the problem.
Open shock rebound 1 click so the rear can recover between whoops instead of riding progressively lower.

The bike may be riding too high, or the fork may be extending and lifting the front out of the rut. Testers consistently report a firm fork and sensitive chassis balance on this generation—don’t start by raising the forks in the clamps.

1. **Check rider sag against Honda’s 105 mm target** with the standard shock spring, wearing your gear. If it measures less, reduce preload to reach 105 mm; don’t add sag blindly. Measure free sag too, to check spring suitability.
2. **If it settles initially, then rises as you open the throttle:** slow fork rebound 1 click from your current position; Honda’s stock reference is **13 out → 12 out**. This helps keep the front settled.
3. **If it stays high and pushes even off the gas:** soften fork compression 1 click instead; stock reference **12 out → 13 out**, helping it settle into the rut. Don’t make both clicker changes together.

Does it stand up as you open the throttle, or while you’re still off the gas?

Meanwhile, repeat one shallow rut five times: sit forward, look through the exit, finish rear braking before leaning, and hold smooth throttle with pressure on the outside peg. Rear-brake dragging can also stand the bike up.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork rebound—only if the front rises as throttle opens:** Turn in 1 click from your current position, equally on both legs. Stock reference: from 13 to 12 clicks out.
- **Fork compression—alternative if it never settles off throttle:** Turn out 1 click from your current position, equally on both legs. Stock reference: from 12 to 13 clicks out.
Check rear ride height first, then separate a fork that never settles from one that rebounds up mid-corner. Those need different clicker changes.

A **shim stack is a pack of thin spring-steel discs that bends under oil pressure**. It controls damping—how much the suspension resists moving, rather than how much weight the spring supports.

- **Diameter and arrangement:** change the leverage oil has on the discs and how progressively they open.
- **Staging:** a deliberately arranged gap can let part of the stack flex before the rest joins in, changing resistance as flow increases.

**Cavitation is when pressure inside the shock drops low enough for tiny vapor bubbles to form in the oil.** When those bubbles reach a higher-pressure area, they collapse.

The shock needs solid oil flowing through its valves to control suspension movement. Bubbles interrupt that flow, so damping can become weak or inconsistent—the rear may feel loose, bounce or kick unexpectedly.

The nitrogen charge helps keep the oil under pressure and resist cavitation. Low gas pressure, poor bleeding during a rebuild or problems with the gas/oil separator can contribute. Air mixed into the oil is technically **aeration**, a different problem with similar effects.

A **bleed circuit** is a small passage that lets suspension oil flow without having to push the main damping shim stack open. It mainly affects how easily the fork or shock starts moving and responds to slower suspension movements—not slower bike speed.

A **bleed shim** creates or meters that bypass at the piston. Depending on the design, it can be a notched shim or a shim arrangement that leaves a small flow path open. It isn’t simply a softer main damping shim.

- **More bleed:** easier initial movement and generally less low-speed damping, but potentially less hold-up under braking or acceleration.
- **Less bleed:** more resistance and chassis control, but potentially a firmer initial feel.

### Check
1. Secure the bike on a lift stand with the front wheel off the ground.
2. With the bars straight, push and pull the fork legs forward and backward. Feel at the steering head for a clunk or movement.
3. Turn the bars slowly lock to lock. Check for roughness or a notch around straight ahead, and make sure cables aren’t causing resistance.

On your 2022 CRF250R, Honda calls for cleaning the air filter **every race or about 2.5 riding hours—and after every moto in dusty conditions**.

In practice, racers commonly start each ride day with a clean, properly oiled filter. That’s the routine I’d use: inspect it between sessions, and swap sooner if it’s loaded with dust, wet or muddy. Don’t wait for the engine to run poorly; filtration can suffer before you feel any power loss.

Keep a second pre-oiled element ready so a dusty day means a quick swap, not a rushed cleaning. If you find dirt inside the intake past the filter, don’t start the engine until it’s cleaned out and the sealing problem is fixed.

**Check tires and wheel alignment first—not clickers.** A sloped road or track can make it drift, but a repeatable pull on level ground is worth checking.

With the engine off and the bike securely supported:
1. Check both tire pressures with a gauge, tire damage, and whether each bead is seated evenly.
2. Check rear-wheel alignment by measuring both swingarm-pivot-to-rear-axle distances; don’t trust the adjuster marks alone.
3. Spin both wheels and check for wobble, bearing play or a brake that binds. Check that the steering moves smoothly without a notch or tight spot.

If it started after a front-wheel change or crash, fork/axle alignment moves high on the list; bent parts are also possible after a crash. **Don’t ride with wheel play, visible wobble, binding steering or impaired braking.**

Did this start after a wheel change or crash? Leave the suspension settings alone until these checks are clear.
A consistent pull needs a tire and wheel-alignment check before suspension changes. Don’t keep testing it hands-off.

Get the bike more upright before feeding in full throttle, and try **one gear taller** through the exit. That turns wheelspin into drive without adding power. Stay seated through the initial drive, grip with your knees and keep your arms loose.

Before changing damping, check the rear tire’s drive edges and cold pressure. Rounded knobs or hardened rubber lose grip even on smooth dirt. With the standard shock spring, Honda’s race-sag baseline is **105 mm**; establish that before chasing clickers.

- **If the rear skips and chatters over exit chop:** soften shock low-speed compression **one click out from its current position**. Honda’s stock reference is **6 out**, so **6 to 7 out** if yours is still stock. This should let the tire follow the bumps.
- If it squats and wallows instead, don’t soften it—that needs more support, not less.

Does it spin on smooth ground too, skip over bumps, or squat as it loses grip? For your first test, repeat the same corner one gear taller with a progressive roll-on; leave the suspension unchanged until you identify which behavior you have.
